en: Shameless and honorless,
You have troubled my heart so deeply.
Licking your sword and kissing your gun,
When you left the Kakan lands,
You vowed that you would stand proud as a hero;
That was the promise you gave.
The honor of a nation is a lofty mountain,
And you came for its sake.
With heroic ambition and a valiant heart,
You meant to crush them,
And said you would open
One of China’s great gates.
You meant to ruin my people
And bring them to their end!”
Thus spoke Chongbilgich,
Boiling and raging in fury,
Thunderously hurling harsh abuse,
Until at last he settled the great account.
“No trace of such a man should remain;
Do not let him rave and babble—
Seize him and cut off his head!”
When their khan shouted from the place of honor,
Could the champions beside him
Possibly stand idle and watch?
Once a man is ruler of the people,
Who dares answer him twice?
The executioners who heard the command
Drew their swords from their sheaths,
Rolled up their strong sleeves,
And ran like wild asses.
One seized his arms and another his legs,
And together they pinned him down.
“This swine has acted insolently,” they said,
“He is the very scourge of the nation;
He is no true kinsman at heart.”
Then they struck off his head with a sword.
Chongbilgich condemned Küлүк,
The man who had spoken the truth,
And snuffed out his fly-like life.
“He died for telling the truth;
We too have come to this,”
The people thought with heavy hearts.
“If he destroys one who did his duty,
Whom will his looming wrath strike next?
If he kills his own kinsman,
To whom will he ever remain faithful?”
Until they returned to Beijing,
Chongbilgich sternly poured out his wrath
On anyone who spoke
And on every champion who came riding,
Threatening to kill anyone who uttered a word,
And made them swear to this.
It became a custom among the Chinese
To answer “mөө” when asked, “Did you see a camel?”
Thus they bound the pledge firmly:
“I did not see it” was the one permitted reply.
From generation to generation,
From clan to clan,
The Chinese people thereafter
Abandoned all talk of the quarrel,
Beginning this custom in that way.
Then Chongbilgich,
Reading his magical divinations
And softly reciting a spell,
Said, “If that Burut comes, let him come—
Why should your warrior brother fear?”
The great Kerik who came from Beijing
Saddled his thoroughbred.
He donned immense armor no bullet could pierce,
Mounted a horse no bullet could overtake,
And took a pine-like spear.
With a cast-iron mace as large as a house,
He said, “Let the frightened Burut flee!
Before my menace and my wrath,
Before my venomous war cry,
Let that Burut, finding no escape,
Sink beneath the earth;
Let the ground sag as I pass!
Let everyone who sees my form
Despair of his precious life,
And flee away in panic!”
His figure appeared stately,
Standing apart from ninety-four others;
He seemed to prop up the sky and move mountains,
As he mounted in fury,
Sucking his pipe and raising an uproar,
Shrouding the face of the earth in steam.
He set a coal in his tinder pipe,
That faithless madman,
Fierce of aspect and mighty in venom,
And put a glowing ember in his pipe,
That expert killer.
He quickly set his shield upon his head,
Beat his war drum and raised a clamor,
Leveled his spear and stirred up strife,
Presenting a sight no man wished to see.
If you hear the sound
Of that madman’s war drum, flee far away!
When it sounds, his champion strikes;
Even an ordinary herd of horses
Breaks away in terror.
That Chinese warrior’s pageantry was immense;
If you ask about his war drum,
It was made from the hide of a wild bull,
And was three fathoms thick.
Everything simply fell apart,
And the breadth of the earth trembled,
When the war drum was beaten hard.
The countless horses in the valley,
The white-faced steeds upon the hills,
That high-spirited madman’s
Racers and swift horses mingled together.
The ground shook and thundered;
Every red-roan, every flat-maned horse,
All of your precious Seytek’s livestock
Panicked together with a roar.
When the horses stampeded,
There were more than a hundred herdsmen;
Some had horses at hand,
While others were caught unawares.
They had eaten the fat barren mares’ foals
And enjoyed comfort winter and summer;
Those overindulged herdsmen
Had still not had their fill of sleep.
The God-forsaken men lay flat,
Wearing trousers without drawstrings,
Stretched out fast asleep.
When the herd stampeded, they leapt up in confusion,
Their trousers still without drawstrings.
They bowed over their waistbands,
And amid such cries,
Their eyes still closed with sleep,
They found and mounted horses.
The herdsmen blustered about,
Striking out with their catch-poles.
Then Chongbilgich,
The most unyielding of men,
Whose fortune was wholly even,
Perfect and lacking nothing,
A mighty and imposing hero,
Stirred up an apocalyptic conflict,
Reached Talas and seized the horses.
Shouting in the Kakan tongue
And assuming a fearsome aspect,
Whenever the herd reached open ground
He went mad and began slaughtering;
He let no wild ass escape,
And shot his bow at anything that fled.
He croaked whenever a raven flew,
Roaring as he poured out his wrath;
The earth broke and stones rolled,
As he shouted the Kakan battle cry.
Dividing the herd into ten,
Harassing every last animal,
He raised a great commotion along the ridge
And drove them onward.
If any horse strayed aside,
He slashed it crosswise and felled it in heaps,
Slaughtering them as he went.
He brought great calamity upon the Kyrgyz
As he went on his way.
Driving off the horses with a roar,
He bellowed menacingly
And summoned his champions.
Swaggering and boasting,
He seized a great many Kyrgyz horses,
And became laden with vast wealth.
Up Suusamyr’s steep ascent,
Straining against the slope,
He dragged them back and forth;
Any foal or yearling unable to walk
He had his champions slaughter.
He drove away the entire herd,
Taking every last horse.
He made the countryside thunder
And set them upon the straight road.
Let us leave that matter here
And begin the tale of the peerless champion Akzholtoi
And the indomitable gray-maned Seytek,
Telling what befell those two.
One herdsman, left for dead,
Brought them word;
Most of the herdsmen
Had been overtaken by death.
Erebai, son of Emil,
Had barely escaped with his life.
His head was split in seven places,
And he had been stabbed in seven places;
His senses failed and his strength was gone,
Yet he escaped when they thought him dead.
He cried out as he went down the Talas,
Calling to his heroes:
“They have reached the very heart of our land together!
They have driven off the whole herd,
Shattering our sleep completely;
They spilled your blood like water
And cut your lives like thread.
They struck your horses upon the hills,
And grievously destroyed your wealth;
They brought disaster upon your lands
And rode straight through your people.
It was the hour of a devastating raid;
These Kalmyks, making everything ring,
Launched their assault.
He is the keen eye
Of the courageous heathen Manchu Chinese,
A hero who never retreats,
And the very embodiment
Of our mortal enemy.
He scoured the land in a dreadful state
And has now ridden away.
He has the thoroughbred Kerik;
If you would fight, that is your foe,
And he alone has the strength of a thousand men.
Would he refrain from bringing grief?
That snarling infidel’s
Battle cry is ‘Kakanchi!’
Would such an enemy stand idle?
That terrifying villain’s
Battle cry is ‘Bakburchun!’
He speaks a strange, rambling tongue;
I understood nothing of it.
My hero Seytek, hear me!
He seized the livestock grazing in the mountains,
And took the lives of multitudes;
He killed the men who guarded the horses,
And took possession of the broad land,
Killing many splendid warriors.
Here I have finally arrived!”
Erebai gasped these words.
“So this is your report, Erebai:
The forces of Beijing have come!”
The power that threw the nation into turmoil—
For from ancient times Great Beijing
Had begun disputes and stirred up strife,
A custom inherited from its forefathers.
The enemy who would never come when sought
Had now come of his own accord to attack;
Without tormenting themselves, they had found him.
Your wish has been fulfilled,
Your enemy has fallen into your hands,
My tiger Seytek, now ride forth,
Good fortune has attended your campaign.
Your vanished enemy has returned,
This alone was your desire,
What you watched for has been granted”—
So saying, Akjoltoy
Mounted the swift steed Külansur,
Knotting up its flowing tail,
Revealing himself as a true hero,
Hearing news of the infidel,
He laughed aloud in delight,
And donned his battle gear.
That noble hero, wolf of war,
Rejoiced at the thought of death,
Through a broad ravine where no hawk flew,
